framework.description: The socio-economic resilience pillar of the UNSDCF is based on policies to support a full-employment economy and to help the country realize the “demographic dividend” by focusing on education and skills development. projects.name: Efficient sewage management to enhance government capacities on climate change adaptation
projects.description:
Based on a partnership with the provincial Water and wastewater Company, the construction of a comprehensive sewage collection network in Kohak was committed by this company, while UNICEF committed to construct the treatment package. Construction of this Sewage Treatment Plant in Kohak village, in Zahak county of Sistan and Baluchestan province, preserves water resources form contamination, benefiting 10,000 local population in Kohak. In collaboration with the project consulting company, the engineering services were successfully completed, encompassing design, calculations, technical specifications, and necessary documentation across structural, mechanical, electrical, and civil disciplines. These deliverables were handed over to the relevant stakeholders, ensuring alignment with project standards and requirements. The design of the system is such that the quality of the treated wastewater would meet the environmental standards set by the Iranian Department of Environmental for the nutrients, heavy metals and microbiological parameters, allowing its outlet to be used for green space irrigation.

A leading company from the Iranian private sector was selected as the contractor for the construction, transportation, installation, and utilization of the sewage treatment plant. The construction of the plant started in the company’s workshop in Isfahan and was completed by September 2024, including all 6 sewage reservoirs, and the package was ready to be transferred to Kohak. 

Following the initial phases, site preparation in Kohak was carried out, ensuring the area was fully prepared for the installation of the treatment package. The workshop mobilization in Kohak was successfully completed in September 2024, including the installation and commissioning of essential machinery, tools, and materials at the project site. This involved setting up prefabricated rooms, pumps, lights, electric panels, and tachometers to support the construction and operation of the facility.

The construction of a concrete platform for the sewage treatment package was the next stage. The platform was successfully completed in October 2024, and the treatment system was transferred from Isfahan to Kohak and installed over it. The contractor utilized the capacity of local concrete delivery companies to facilitate the construction process.

.Day-to-day resident technical supervision during the execution process was carried out by a qualified consulting company from the private sector, contracted by the provincial WWC. UNICEF, in collaboration with the provincial WWC, also provided high-level technical oversight of the project in coordination with the consulting company.

As a result of this support, the water quality of aquifers (Chahnimes) will be improved, leading to improved water quality for the Niatak Refugee settlement which is supplied through this wate rresource and environmental sanitation in areas will be improved, leading to the advanced well-being of the refugees and the people from the host communities living in this area. This project was completed by the end of December 2024. The commissioning and utilization was followed in 2025. This is the last component of the joint initiative between the Republic of Korea and UNICEF Iran with the current funding.

Iran is grappling with a multitude of severe climate-related issues. These include floods, droughts, desertification, dust storms, and declining biodiversity. The economic impact of natural disasters in Iran is predominantly from hydro-meteorological hazards, such as floods and droughts, accounting for about 70% of long-term damages, with the remaining 30% attributed to earthquakes and other disasters. Floods regularly afflict different parts of the country, placing Iran among the top 20 nations worldwide in terms of flood damage.

Component 1: Flood Inundation Mapping and Risk Assessment in a Selected Basin for Early Warning System Development
Component 2: Agricultural Drought Risk Assessment in the Selected Basin

projects.name: Improving climate resilience in schools
projects.description:
Improving climate resilience in schools of 2 provinces hit by climate change, namely Sistan and Baluchestan and Khorasan Razavi
WASH rehabilitation:  

At the beginning of the project, UNICEF worked with regional experts from MoE and the Organization for Development, Renovation and Equipping of Schools (ODRES) to identify schools requiring support in sanitation facilities and water hygiene in the provinces of Khorasan Razavi and Sistan and Baluchestan, which host significant numbers of Afghan students. 

The Tabadkan educational region in Khorasan Razavi Province, one of UNICEF’s target areas, is among the most important educational areas hosting refugee students. According to available statistics, 29,000 Afghan students out of a total student population of 165,000 benefit from MoE educational services in this region. Some schools in the area have student populations that are up to 80 per cent Afghan. These areas, which also host internal migrants from eastern parts of the country, other parts of the province and the city of Mashhad, face substantial infrastructural challenges and are considered deprived areas based on relevant deprivation indices. 

In Khorasan Razavi Province, rehabilitation of WASH facilities was implemented in Mashhad’s Tabadkan and District No. 5, covering a total of 15 schools. Through these interventions, 3,104 refugee students, including 1,847 girls and 1,257 boys, and 7,162 Iranian students, including 3,393 girls and 3,769 boys, benefited from improved WASH infrastructure. Overall, 10,266 students gained access to safer and more functional water, sanitation and hygiene facilities. The activities focused on restoring and upgrading school WASH systems to ensure safer water access and improved sanitation conditions. 

In Sistan and Baluchestan Province, rehabilitation activities were carried out in the cities of Zahedan and Zabol, reaching 18 schools. These interventions benefited 1,720 refugee students, including 1,268 girls and 452 boys, and 11,031 Iranian students, including 7,342 girls and 3,689 boys. In total, 12,751 students were supported through the rehabilitation of WASH facilities. The works significantly improved water supply systems, sanitation facilities and overall hygiene conditions in the targeted schools. 

Based on the results of ongoing needs assessments during implementation, UNICEF complemented this project through other funding sources by procuring and installing essential WASH items in both provinces. This support covered 87 schools, including 14 in Khorasan Razavi and 73 in Sistan and Baluchestan. A total of 4,041 refugee students, including 1,872 girls and 2,169 boys, and 43,562 Iranian students, including 19,509 girls and 24,053 boys, benefited from the provision of water pumps, water tanks, water purifiers and water coolers. Overall, these procurement activities supported 47,603 students, strengthening access to safe drinking water and enhancing the functionality and sustainability of school WASH facilities in both provinces. 

Through the combined implementation of WASH rehabilitation and the procurement and installation of essential WASH items, the project reached a total of 120 schools across Khorasan Razavi and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces. In total, 70,620 students benefited from improved WASH services, including 8,865 refugee students, of whom 4,987 were girls and 3,878 were boys, and 61,755 Iranian students, of whom 30,244 were girls and 31,511 were boys. These interventions significantly enhanced access to safe water and sanitation facilities, contributing to healthier and more supportive learning environments in the targeted schools.

projects.name: Strengthening national capacity on implementing Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement (WASH FIT) to improve quality of care in health care facilities (WHO and UNICEF)
projects.description:
"This programme intervention strengthens the capacity of experts of Ministry of Health and Medical Education (MOHME), universities of Medical Education and environmental health technicians of healthcare facilities in a training for trainers (TOT) workshop run jointly by UNICEF (regional and national), WHO (regional and national), and MOHME staff for implementing and coordinating WASH in Healthcare Facilities programmes/initiatives. The workshop enhanced the participants' skills and knowledge in supporting their countries in implementing the WASH FIT approach, gaining practical insights from regional and international experts, and sharing past experiences and lessons learned. Through this intervention, MoHME was further supported to institutionalize the WASH-FIT approach within the national health system, ensuring its systematic integration into policies, standards, and routine practices across healthcare facilities."
Between 11 and 15 October, environmental health experts from 40 universities of medical sciences across 25 provinces participated in a national training of trainers (ToT), organized jointly by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education (MoHME), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF).

The workshop strengthened the capacity of participants to lead improvements in water supply, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), waste management and cleaning services in health facilities, essential elements of infection prevention, patient safety and quality care.
The training combined classroom learning with field visits and practical group exercises, allowing participants to apply the WASH FIT methodology in real-world settings. Facilitators from WHO and UNICEF noted the high level of professionalism and engagement, describing it as one of the most successful WASH FIT trainings conducted in the Region.

WASH FIT is a risk-based, iterative management tool developed by WHO and UNICEF to help health facilities identify hazards, prioritize improvements and monitor progress. Its adoption can reduce health care-associated infections, improve maternal and newborn care and build resilience against climate and health threats. In use in more than 50 countries, it enables health facilities to identify risks, plan and prioritize low-cost improvements and monitor progress over time.

The initiative builds on the Islamic Republic of Iran’s ongoing efforts to improve WASH in health care, including a 2021 baseline assessment of 742 facilities and a costed national roadmap developed with WHO support. It aligns with the WHO–MoHME 5-year strategic framework on environmental and occupational health and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for Iran.

The workshop concluded with a high-level ceremony at Shahid Rajaei Heart Hospital attended by senior officials from MoHME, the Ministry of Energy, Presidential Department of Environment, WHO, UNICEF and the United Nations.

Young Water Guardians: How Students in Birjand Are Leading the Way in Water Conservation

When my colleague and I arrived in Birjand on a crisp December morning, we were welcomed by a team of experts from the Water and Water waste Company (WWC), eager to take us to a special event - the “Water Celebration.” This UNICEF-supported initiative builds on long-standing educational programs about water conservation, implemented jointly by the Ministry of Energy and the Ministry of Education. As we drove through the dry landscape of Birjand, it was clear why such efforts were essential: every drop of water mattered.
In the car, WWC experts explained that renovating old water facilities and raising awareness about responsible water use were top priorities. That’s why UNICEF, through its WASH and Social and Behavior Change (SBC) programmes, had stepped in not only to upgrade water taps, drinking fountains, and restroom facilities in schools but also to launch an educational campaign called “Water for all, all for Water”. This campaign reached 700 students across three primary schools, engaging them as active participants in water conservation through the “Water-Guardians” initiative.

A Celebration of Water Awareness
Upon arrival at Sanderos School in Birjand, we stepped were welcomed into a vibrant celebration hall filled with energy and enthusiasm. More than 340 Iranian and Afghan students, all wearing colorful caps adorned with water drop symbols, held educational pamphlets about responsible water use. Around the hall, students’ artwork lined the walls, showcasing creative expressions of the importance of water. A lively water-themed song played in the background, setting the tone for an engaging event.
The celebration featured a variety of activities, students shared traditional stories about water conservation, animated characters highlighted the consequences of water waste, and winners of a water themed painting competition were announced. The event ended with a powerful call to action from school authorities, encouraging students to become agents of change in their families and communities.
After the event, we toured the newly renovated water facilities, including modernized drinking fountains, upgraded taps, and repaired restrooms facilities - supported by UNICEF. It was heartwarming to see children excited about these improvements. “Upgrading the taps and water facilities has made a big difference. Now, there’s no more leaking water!” shared Ahmad, a third-grade student. “Some of us used to worry about the old taps wasting water,” added Pooya, another student. Their words reaffirmed the impact of UNICEF’s support—not just in improving infrastructure but in fostering a sense of responsibility among students.

Students as Water Ambassadors[MN1.1]
The “Water-Guardians” initiative aims to empower students to take an active role in water conservation. Through training sessions with WWC experts and educational materials, children learn how to advocate for responsible water use, both in school and at home. Recognizing the potential of this initiative, school authorities and government officials expressed their commitment to expanding it. “Students are the best ambassadors for water conservation. Their engagement will not only shape their behavior but also influence their families and communities,” said Mr. Asemani, the school principal.

Looking Ahead: A Student-Led Water Movement; Closing ceremony 
UNICEF with the cooperation of the Ministry of Energy and WWC plans to support strengthening and[MN2.1] expanding the “Water-Guardians” initiative across more schools in 2025, creating a network of student volunteers who receive educational briefings from WWC and committed to water preservation. The closing ceremony for the “Water for All, All for Water” campaign that was planned to reach 5000 students in primary school across the province,  happened in early February with high level participation from Ministry of Energy, UNICEF and national WWC representatives, Member of Parliament for South Khorasan and Governor General of the town and most importantly 400 school boys and girls students in Nehbandan town. The ceremony was an opportunity to underscore the crucial role of children in water conservation efforts, the importance of water education and awareness raising in the communities by students, connecting schools to WWC and calling for expanding this successful campaign to other provinces. An exhibition of hand-made crafts and paintings by students with the theme of not wasting water was an eye-catching part of the event that was well planned and displayed conjointly with the music singing, role playing, interactive questions and answers with the students by authorities, hands-on guidance for appropriate behaviours that leads to saving water at home and school, and many more engaging activities. Students were fully engaged and attentive to the ceremony while exchanging and playing with one another in the hall. The event was followed by a planning meeting between UNICEF and WWC on how to take forward the initiative and involve more sectors. This has been the first time that UNICEF’s contribution in awareness raising for water conservation programmes among the students in schools occurred.  
As our visit came to an end, I was convinced that investing in young people as water stewards can create lasting change. With the right education and support, students can be the driving force behind a more sustainable future for Iran’s water resources.

projects.name: Improvement of water consumption habits and management
projects.description:
Identification of household water consumption behaviors and practices, and development of a community-based action plan (to promote improved habits and water consumption management in urban and rural households of Yasuj) was the primary purpose of this project.
Project proceedings: The project adopted a **concurrent mixed-methods approach**, combining quantitative and qualitative research to develop evidence-based and context-specific recommendations for reducing household water consumption. The quantitative component consisted of a structured household survey of **100 urban and rural residents aged 15 years and above**, selected through multi-stage cluster sampling to ensure representation across gender, age groups, place of residence, and persons with disabilities. The qualitative component included **40 in-depth interviews** (20 community members and 20 water experts and key informants), followed by **two two-day participatory consultation workshops** involving **20 participants** (10 community representatives and 10 water experts) to validate findings and co-develop practical behaviour change interventions. Quantitative data were analysed using statistical methods, while qualitative data underwent grounded theory analysis. The combined findings informed the development of a community-based behavioural intervention package and an operational action plan for sustainable water demand management.   

Summary of Results

The study found that excessive household water consumption is driven primarily by deeply rooted daily habits and social norms rather than a lack of awareness alone. High-consumption practices—such as prolonged showers, leaving taps running, washing courtyards and vehicles with hoses, inefficient irrigation of home gardens, and improper use of household appliances—are reinforced by cultural perceptions of cleanliness, comfort, and convenience, as well as by climatic conditions, housing characteristics, and economic factors.

The findings also showed that knowledge alone is insufficient to achieve sustained behaviour change. Participants emphasized the need for practical, locally relevant communication, family-based interventions, and school-based education, with children serving as effective agents of change within households. Positive incentives, such as rewards for low water consumption, were perceived as more motivating than punitive measures alone.

Clear differences were identified between urban and rural communities. Urban households reported higher sensitivity to water shortages due to pressure reductions and service interruptions, while rural households, with greater access to natural water sources, often perceived water as abundant and showed lower sensitivity to conservation. Water use patterns also differed, highlighting the need for context-specific interventions rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Overall, the results indicate that effective water demand management requires integrated behaviour change strategies that combine awareness raising with practical guidance, social norm change, incentives, improved access to water-saving technologies, and interventions tailored to local socio-cultural and environmental contexts.
